title: Sri Rasika Raya
html:
The Deity of Gangamata

In Puri, at the abode of Gangamata Gosvamini on the bank of the Shvetaganga, Sri Krishna accepts service as Sri Rasika Raya. The biographies call Him Sri Rasika Raya, Sri Rasikaraya and, reverently, Sri Rasika Raya Jiu. Today in Gangamata's matha He is served together with Sri Radha, and the Divine Couple is known as Sri Sri Radha-Rasikaraya. He is Krishna Himself: when Gangamata first saw Him, she received the darshan of Sri Govinda, and when she heard His word in a dream, she marvelled that Sri Hari Himself wished to eat from her hands1. Gangamata's matha stands where the house of Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya once was: so the biographies say, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati says the same in the “Anubhashya”2.

All that is known of Him took place after Sri Chaitanya's disappearance, in the days of Gangamata Gosvamini. The “Chaitanya-charitamrita” itself and the other primary sources do not speak of Him. But Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in his “Anubhashya” on the “Chaitanya-charitamrita”, listing the spiritual succession of the Gangamata Matha, writes of Gangamata that, having brought the Deity Sri Rasikaraya from Krishna Mishra of Jaipur, she opened His service in Purushottama, in the house of Sarvabhauma3. The detailed story of Him has been preserved by the biographies of Gangamata.

In a brahmana's house in Jaipur

Sri Rasika Raya formerly resided in Jaipur, in Rajasthan, in the house of a brahmana named Sri Chandra Sharma, a pious devotee. But the brahmana was poor and could not serve Him as was fitting4.

Jagannatha's command

Then Sri Jagannatha came to the brahmana in a dream and bade him hand Rasika Raya over to Gangamata. “Rasika Raya is not served properly in your house,” the Lord said. “Take Him quickly to Gangamata, who lives on the bank of the Shvetaganga in Sri Purushottama-kshetra; otherwise misfortune will befall you”5.

Having received the Lord's command, the brahmana set out at once, taking Rasika Raya with him, and came to Sri Kshetra. There he sought out Gangamata, came to her door and asked her to accept the service of Rasika Raya6.

The refusal and the night in the tulasi grove

Gangamata was overjoyed to see the Deity. But when she had heard the brahmana out, she declined: “I am a beggar woman and live on alms (madhukari). How can I serve Him? Take Him back — do not make me an offender”7.

The brahmana was at a loss. He pondered for a long time, and at last, at night, he left Sri Rasika Raya in the tulasi grove by her abode and went away — he all but fled. That same night Rasika Raya Himself came to Gangamata in a dream: “I have come here to accept your service. The brahmana left Me in the tulasi grove and went away. I have not eaten anything yet — feed Me”8.

The first night of service

The dream filled her with wonder. Thrilling with love, she bathed in haste, went to the tulasi grove and saw Sri Rasika Raya there. Offering Him full obeisances (dandavat-pranama), she carried Him into the house, at once gave Him His bath and offered Him bhoga. And Gangamata saw the hungry Rasika Raya swiftly partake of all she had offered; she wept tears of joy. Then she spread a new cloth and laid the Thakura down to rest.

In the morning the devotees came. Seeing Sri Rasika Raya, they were astonished. From then on Gangamata, with great love, cooked for Him rice, vegetable dishes (vyanjana), cakes (pitha) and drinks (pana) and fed Him9. His service took up four praharas of her every day.

Service on alms

For some time Gangamata served Rasika Raya with whatever she received as alms. The years went by, and the labour grew ever harder for her. Sri Rasika Raya saw her toil — and He Himself so arranged things that wealthy merchants began to bring the supplies for His service. Thus the Lord, in His love for His maidservant, Himself takes care of her service.

“Come to My abode”

When Gangamata grew old, she began to feel that faults were creeping into her service. She begged Rasika Raya's forgiveness and said that she no longer had the strength to serve Him. Rasika Raya answered her in a dream: “I am pleased with your service. Do not grieve — serve a little longer.”

Some time passed, and again she told Rasika Raya that she no longer wished to remain here — if only, on leaving the body, she might go with His name on her lips. This was not weariness of life but longing for Him. And Rasika Raya replied: “Do not worry about anything. Place My service in the hands of a worthy disciple and come to My abode (dhama).”

Then Gangamata entrusted the service of Rasika Raya to a quiet, peaceful devotee, Banamali Dasa; by Rasika Raya's words, he was her disciple10. In the succession of the matha given by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, Sri Vanamali is named immediately after Gangamata — in all likelihood this is he11. She herself, contemplating the feet of Sri Rasika Raya and His beauty, departed from this world and entered the eternal lila at the age of one hundred and twenty, in 1721, on the ashvina-shukla-ekadashi12.

In Gangamata's matha today

Today five Divine Couples reside in Gangamata's matha: Sri Sri Radha-Rasikaraya, Radha-Shyamasundara, Radha-Madana-mohana, Radha-Vinoda and Radha-Ramana. Here too are Sri Damodara-shalagrama, whom Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya served, the dancing Sri Gaura, and Naru-Gopala (Laddu-Gopala). The sources name neither the year in which Sri Rasika Raya came to Puri nor the day of the festival of His appearance; nor are any of His days found in the Vaishnava calendar of Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Significance

The story of Sri Rasika Raya shows how the Lord Himself chooses His servant. It is not wealth that draws Him, nor splendour of service: He came to the poor Gangamata, who lived on alms, and Himself asked her to feed Him. When the service became hard for her, He Himself provided the supplies; when she grew weary, He comforted her and extended her service; and when the time came, He called her to His own abode.

Notes

  1. “Govinda” here is simply a name of Krishna. This is not Sri Govindadeva of Rupa Gosvami, although Sri Rasika Raya did come from Jaipur, where Govindadeva now resides. Nor should He be confused with Sri Rasikaraya, the Deity of Chandrashekhara Vaidya of Shrikhanda.
  2. The biographies place Gangamata's abode on the bank of the Shvetaganga; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in the “Anubhashya” on Madhya 6.8, writes that Sarvabhauma lived south of the Sri Mandira, in Balukhanda, on the bank of Markandeya-saras, and that this house is now known as the Gangamata Matha.
  3. “Anubhashya” on Adi 8.59–60. The biographies tell it otherwise: they name Sri Rasika Raya's former servant as the brahmana Chandra Sharma, and say that the brahmana himself brought the Deity to Gangamata. Where exactly Gangamata received the Deity, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta does not specify.
  4. So in the detailed account of Sri Rasika Raya. According to other accounts, including one of the biographies, the brahmana had committed an offence in service (seva-aparadha), and for that reason he was left without descendants. The sources speak here of the consequences of an offence in the service of the Deity, not of a worldly curse; the brahmana's piety is stressed all the same.
  5. So in the detailed account of Sri Rasika Raya. According to other accounts, Jagannatha told the brahmana: “Give the service of this Deity to Gangamata, and your offence and fear will go”; or: thus he would be freed from the consequences of his offences.
  6. According to one account, the brahmana brought Rasika Raya together with Sri Radharani and wished to entrust Gangamata with the service of both Deities; the others say not a word about Her. Today in the matha They are served as the Divine Couple — Sri Sri Radha-Rasikaraya.
  7. According to other accounts, Gangamata declined because she could not maintain service on a royal scale (raja-seva).
  8. Other accounts are briefer: Rasika Raya Himself told her in a dream to accept Him and serve Him. The dreams in this story are not visions that merely “seemed” to be, but His will and His direct word, just as was Jagannatha's command to the brahmana.
  9. According to other accounts, as bidden in the dream, Gangamata in great joy held a festival of the appearance (prakatya-mahotsava) of the Deities; in the detailed account of Sri Rasika Raya, instead of a festival there are the night feeding and the devotees' astonishment in the morning.
  10. The source does not say outright that Banamali Dasa was her disciple; this follows from Rasika Raya's instruction to hand the service over to a worthy disciple.
  11. “Anubhashya” on Adi 8.59–60: in this list Gangamata is followed by Sri Vanamali, then Bhagavan Dasa, Madhusudana Dasa and others, down to the present mahanta of the matha. That Vanamali is the same Banamali Dasa is not said outright; it follows from the name (in Bengali “Banamali” and “Vanamali” are spelt alike) and from his place immediately after her.
  12. According to the matha itself, Gangamata appeared in 1601, on the jyeshtha-shukla-dashami, and entered the eternal lila in 1721; this agrees with her hundred and twenty years. The Vaishnava calendar of Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math marks her appearance day — the Gaura-dashami of the month of Trivikrama (jyeshtha-shukla-dashami); the day of her departure (the Gaura-ekadashi of the month of Padmanabha) is not in the calendar.
